title: Memory Hierarchy
summary: No single memory is both fast and big. Learn how systems stack small-fast and big-slow memory into levels that feel fast overall.

blocks.markdown:
The **memory hierarchy** is a stack of memory types, from tiny and fast at the top to huge and slow at the bottom.

- Fast memory (like **registers**) is small and expensive per byte.
- Big memory (like **disk**) is cheap per byte but slow.
- The CPU can't get both in one memory, so it uses several, layered.
- Done well, the system *feels* almost as fast as the top layer.

There's a hard physical trade-off: **speed costs area and power**.

- Fast circuits need more transistors per bit, so they stay small and pricey — that's why registers are only a few dozen values.
- Slow storage packs bits densely and cheaply, so it can be huge — that's why a disk can hold terabytes.
- No technology gives both, so systems combine several, each covering the gap the previous one leaves.

blocks.subTitle: Registers
blocks.markdown:
**Registers** are storage slots built directly into the CPU.

- Accessed in about **1 CPU cycle** — the fastest memory that exists.
- Only a few dozen exist, each holding one value (like an integer or address).
- Every instruction the CPU runs reads or writes registers directly.

blocks.subTitle: Cache — L1, L2, L3
blocks.markdown:
**Cache** is small, fast memory that keeps a copy of data the CPU is likely to reuse soon.

- **L1** — closest to the core, a few dozen KB, ~1-4 cycles.
- **L2** — bigger, slightly slower, a few hundred KB to 1MB.
- **L3** — shared across cores, several MB, tens of cycles.
- Smaller cache = faster but pricier per byte; L1 < L2 < L3 in speed and size, in that order.

blocks.subTitle: Main memory (DRAM)
blocks.markdown:
**Main memory** is **DRAM** (Dynamic RAM) — the system's RAM, measured in GB.

- Far bigger than cache, but a miss there costs roughly **100+ cycles**, not tens.
- Holds the working set of running programs — code and data in active use.
- Volatile: contents vanish when power is lost, unlike disk or SSD.

blocks.subTitle: SSD and disk
blocks.markdown:
**SSD/disk** is the bottom of the hierarchy — permanent storage that survives power loss.

- **SSD** (flash-based) — microseconds per access, TB-scale, no moving parts.
- **HDD** (spinning disk) — milliseconds per access, cheapest per byte, biggest capacity.
- Both are orders of magnitude slower than DRAM, but hold far more data for far less money.

The hierarchy as a pyramid — narrow and fast at the top, wide and slow at the bottom.

blocks.subTitle: Rough numbers
blocks.markdown:
Approximate figures to anchor the scale — exact numbers vary by hardware.

| Level | Speed | Typical size |
|---|---|---|
| Register | ~1 cycle | Bytes |
| L1 cache | ~1-4 cycles | ~32-64 KB |
| DRAM | ~100+ cycles | GBs |
| SSD | ~microseconds | TBs |

Each step down is roughly an order of magnitude slower and bigger.

The hierarchy only helps because real programs show the **principle of locality**: they don't access memory randomly.

- If a program touched every address equally often, keeping a small fast cache would be pointless.
- Instead, programs reuse a small set of addresses again and again over any short stretch of time.
- This pattern is what caches are built to exploit. See [cache-fundamentals](cache-fundamentals).

blocks.subTitle: Temporal vs spatial
blocks.markdown:
Locality comes in two flavors.

- **Temporal locality** — data used once will likely be used again soon (a loop variable, re-read each pass).
- **Spatial locality** — data near a used address will likely be used next (array elements stored side by side).
- Caches exploit both: they keep recent data (temporal) and fetch whole nearby blocks, not single bytes (spatial).

Data doesn't jump straight from disk to a register — it moves **level by level**.

- A miss at one level pulls a chunk of data up from the level below it, not just the one byte asked for.
- That chunk is called a **block** (in cache) or a **page** (in main memory) — sized to exploit spatial locality.
- Once loaded, nearby future accesses hit the faster level instead of repeating the slow trip.

blocks.subTitle: Hit, miss, effective access time
blocks.markdown:
A **hit** finds data already at the fast level; a **miss** means fetching it from a slower one.

- **Effective access time** is the real-world average: mostly fast hits, occasionally a slow miss.
- Intuition: if 90% of accesses hit a fast cache and 10% miss to slow memory, the average stays close to the fast time — not the slow one.
- A high **hit rate** is what makes the whole hierarchy feel fast.

The **memory wall** is the growing gap between CPU speed and memory speed.

- CPU speeds grew far faster than DRAM speeds for decades — CPUs now finish thousands of cycles in the time one DRAM access takes.
- Without caches, the fast CPU would sit idle most of the time waiting on memory.
- The hierarchy exists largely *because of* this wall — it hides slow memory behind fast, well-used caches.

Common mistakes:

- **"More cache always helps."** Bigger cache is slower per access — size is a trade-off, not free.
- **"Registers and cache are the same thing."** Registers are CPU-internal and named by instructions; cache is transparent and addressed like memory.
- **"RAM and storage are interchangeable."** DRAM is volatile working memory; SSD/disk is where data survives power-off.

blocks.subTitle: Why a hierarchy
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: Why do computers use a memory hierarchy instead of one big fast memory?**

Because fast memory is physically expensive and can't scale to large sizes — building all of RAM out of register-speed circuits would be unaffordable and huge. Layering small-fast on top of big-slow, and exploiting locality, gives near-top speed at bottom-level cost.

blocks.subTitle: Temporal vs spatial
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: Explain temporal vs spatial locality with an example.**

Temporal: a loop counter is read every iteration — reused again and again soon. Spatial: looping over an array touches adjacent memory addresses one after another. Caches keep recent data (temporal) and fetch whole blocks around an address (spatial) to exploit both.

blocks.subTitle: The memory wall
blocks.markdown:
**Q: What is the memory wall?**

The widening speed gap between CPUs and DRAM — CPU performance grew much faster than memory performance over the decades. It means a CPU stalled on a memory miss wastes huge numbers of cycles, which is exactly why multi-level caches became essential.

blocks.subTitle: Ordering the levels
blocks.markdown:
**Q: Order the memory levels from fastest to slowest.**

Registers, then L1 cache, then L2, then L3, then main memory (DRAM), then SSD, then disk. Speed and cost drop together going down; size grows going down.

blocks.subTitle: Why not all fast memory
blocks.markdown:
**Q: Why not just build all memory as fast as registers?**

Cost and physics — register-speed circuits need more transistors per bit, so they're expensive and don't scale to gigabytes. It would also draw far more power and chip area than is practical, so systems layer memory instead.

blocks.subTitle: Hit rate impact
blocks.markdown:
**Q: Why does a small change in cache hit rate matter so much?**

Because a miss costs so much more than a hit — often 100x or more. Dropping from a 99% to a 95% hit rate multiplies the miss count fivefold, which can noticeably slow the whole system despite looking like a small percentage change.
